title: Give in secret (Matthew 6:1–4)
hookLine: don't let your left hand know what your right hand is doing

lines: A TINY WISH TO BE SEEN.
A TRUMPET IN FRONT OF THE GIFT.
cards: A coffee paid for, for the stranger behind you in line. Trash picked up in the stairwell. A small kindness nobody saw.
And then, sometimes, a tiny wish that someone had: that it might come up in conversation, or that the person might turn around in time to see who it was.
It's an old and very human wish, and Jesus, in the middle of the Sermon on the Mount, puts his finger right on it. He describes someone giving to the poor with a trumpet blowing in front of them.

teach.b: Alms is an old English word for gifts to the poor. It comes, through Latin, from the Greek eleēmosynē, which grows out of eleos, mercy. So alms are mercy you can hold in your hand.
The same root sits in the old church cry Kyrie eleison: Lord, have mercy. In Matthew chapter six, Jesus doesn't say whether to give. He takes that for granted, and talks about how.
In the King James words: "when thou doest thine alms, do not sound a trumpet before thee, as the hypocrites do." Nobody is sure anyone literally blew a trumpet.
Some readers think it's a picture, a joke even, like don't toot your own horn. Others connect it to the trumpet-shaped offering boxes said to stand in the Temple.
Either way, the point lands: people who give for applause get the applause, and that's all they get.
Then the strangest line: "let not thy left hand know what thy right hand doeth." You can't hide something from your own hand.

teach.h: A GIFT THAT BUYS NOTHING BACK.
teach.b: That's the point: a gift so quiet that even you barely make a story of it.

teach.h: THY FATHER WHICH SEETH IN SECRET.
teach.b: "That thine alms may be in secret: and thy Father which seeth in secret himself shall reward thee openly." Christians have found plenty of quiet ways: the anonymous envelope, the unsigned check, groceries left on a porch.
Jews have a long tradition here too; the medieval teacher Maimonides ranked a gift where giver and receiver don't know each other near the very top. The idea underneath is freeing.
A secret gift can't buy anything back: no thanks, no reputation, no story to tell.

how: Many Christians give to the poor quietly, through unsigned gifts, anonymous envelopes or church funds that keep donors' names private, taking Jesus's words about secret giving as their guide.

games.why: "let not thy left hand know what thy right hand doeth." the gift is meant to be so quiet that even you barely make a story of it.

practice: Let one gift come to mind that nobody could trace back to you: a few dollars in a jar, an unsigned kind review for a small business, a bill paid quietly for someone who's short.
Notice the small tug to tell someone, and let it pass. If you pray, offer the gift to God, who sees in secret; if you don't, let it be yours alone.

wordCard.voice: Alms. Gifts to the poor, from a Greek word rooted in mercy. Jesus asks for them quietly, without the trumpet.

orig.note: Greek: mercy shown, a gift to the poor. the English word alms comes from it, through Latin.

carryVoice: Your line: let it stay secret. Not even the group chat needs to know. One hundred thirty-three days, and counting.
